a: not even found among the Gentiles
p: The KJV says such sin is not even 'named' among the Gentiles; the critical editions have no such word.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (no verb; 'such sexual sin as not even among the Gentiles')
readings.en: not even among the Gentiles
readings.plain: not even found among the Gentiles

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV) add 'is named' (the editions' word list shows it in both)
readings.en: not even named among the Gentiles
readings.plain: not even named among the Gentiles

why: The Plain follows the shorter text, which every critical edition prints. A copyist could easily have added a verb to complete the sentence, because the Greek has none. The sense is the same either way: this sin is unheard of among the Gentiles.
b: The words in the Plain, "found," fill the gap in the shorter text the way English requires. The Byzantine and Textus Receptus addition "is named" gives the KJV's "not so much as named among the Gentiles."

a: the name of our Lord Jesus
p: The Byzantine text adds 'Christ' in 5:4, twice.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 (with 'Jesus' alone, 'our Lord Jesus' twice)
readings.en: of our Lord Jesus
readings.plain: the name of our Lord Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV); the first 'Christ' is also in Tyndale House GNT, as the editions' table shows
readings.en: of our Lord Jesus Christ
readings.plain: the name of our Lord Jesus Christ

why: The Plain follows the shorter reading found in the SBLGNT and NA28. Scribes tend to lengthen the names of Jesus, and the longer form is the more familiar one. The editions disagree only about the first "Christ."
b: The same kind of addition occurs in 5:5 ("Jesus") and 6:11 ("Christ"). No difference of meaning results.

a: the day of the Lord
t: 'The day of the Lord' or 'of the Lord Jesus'?
p: Some Greek editions add 'Jesus', as the KJV does.

readings.w: SBLGNT and NA28 ('the day of the Lord')
readings.en: the day of the Lord
readings.plain: the day of the Lord

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV) add 'Jesus'
readings.en: the day of the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: the day of the Lord Jesus

why: The Plain follows the shorter reading. It may seem odd for Paul to speak of "the Lord" without a name, but "the day of the Lord" is the Old Testament phrase, and a scribe would be likely to add the name to make clear who is meant.
b: The editions' table gives the pattern; no manuscripts are named here.

a: has been slaughtered
p: The KJV says Christ our Passover was sacrificed 'for us'; those two words are not in the critical editions.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: has been sacrificed (slaughtered)
readings.plain: has been slaughtered

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV) add 'for us'
readings.en: has been sacrificed for us
readings.plain: has been slaughtered for us

why: The Plain follows the shorter text. The longer reading explains what the verb means, which is typical of a scribe's addition; the sense is already in the sentence.

a: God judges those outside.
t: 'God judges' or 'God will judge' the outsiders?
p: Editions differ on whether the verb is present or future.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (present tense, 'judges')
readings.en: judges
readings.plain: God judges those outside.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (future, 'will judge')
readings.en: will judge
readings.plain: God will judge those outside.

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT. The present tense can mean a general truth, God's constant right. The future tense points to the last judgment. The two are not far apart in sense. The two forms differ only in accent.
b: The two forms differ only in accent, and the editions choose. The SBLGNT also prints a question mark (the Greek semicolon) after the verb, so that its text can be read "Does God judge those outside?" The Plain reads it as a statement. This entry names editions only.

a: Remove the evil person from among yourselves.
p: The KJV reads 'Therefore put away'; the Byzantine text has 'and you will remove.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (imperative, no connecting word)
readings.orig: ἐξάρατε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν
readings.en: Remove the evil person from among yourselves
readings.plain: Remove the evil person from among yourselves.

readings.w: The KJV's English: 'Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person' (a command with a connecting word; the word list does not show which Greek text the KJV translates)
readings.orig: ἐξάρατε οὖν τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν
readings.en: Therefore remove the evil person from among yourselves
readings.plain: So remove the evil person from among yourselves.

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (the word list shows 'and' in both): future with 'and'. Only this form is a prediction
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξαρεῖτε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν
readings.en: And you will remove the evil person from among yourselves
readings.plain: And you will remove the evil person from among yourselves.

why: The Plain follows the command without a connecting word, which the critical editions print. The KJV's "Therefore" is a third form, a command with a connecting word added. The future form reads as a statement of what the church will do, and a copyist could have changed Paul's command to that form. This entry names editions only.

a: the name of the Lord Jesus
t: 'The Lord Jesus' or 'the Lord Jesus Christ'?
p: NA28 and some other editions add 'Christ'; the SBLGNT, the Byzantine text and the KJV do not.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: of the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: the name of the Lord Jesus

readings.w: NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: of the Lord Jesus Christ
readings.plain: the name of the Lord Jesus Christ

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT. This is one of a few places where the NA28 text is longer than the SBLGNT. The "Christ" could have come from the commoner full title.
b: The KJV's "Lord Jesus" here is not a sign of a Byzantine addition. The editions' table shows the Byzantine text and the SBLGNT agree against NA28.

a: So bring glory to God in your body.
t: A longer ending in the KJV
p: The KJV adds 'and in your spirit, which are God's'; this is in the Byzantine text but not in the critical editions.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
readings.en: glorify God in your body
readings.plain: So bring glory to God in your body.

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ὑμῶν, ἅτινά ἐστιν τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's
readings.plain: So bring glory to God in your body and in your spirit, which belong to God.

why: The Plain follows the shorter text. The longer reading fits the sense but is probably an expansion: the argument of 6:12-20 is about the body, and a scribe added the spirit so that the whole person belonged to God.
b: The added words are the source of the KJV's "and in your spirit, which are God's." They do not teach anything unlike Paul's other letters.

a: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.
t: Quoted slogan or Paul's own words?
p: The Greek has no quotation marks. The Plain marks 7:1 as a Corinthian saying; the same words can be read as Paul's own.

readings.w: The Plain's punctuation (an editorial choice; ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks)
readings.en: It is good for a man not to touch a woman (quoted from the Corinthians' letter; the Plain puts quotation marks around it)
readings.plain: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.

readings.w: The reading with no quotation marks, as in the KJV (Paul speaks in his own voice and goes on to qualify it)
readings.en: It is good for a man not to touch a woman (Paul's own counsel)
readings.plain: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.

why: The Plain follows the view that Paul is quoting the Corinthians' letter and then answering it (7:2-7). That is an interpretation, not a difference in the Greek text, and the older view that the sentence is Paul's own counsel is also held. Every pair of quotation marks of this kind in the Plain (6:12, 6:13, 7:1, 8:1, 8:4, 8:10) is an editorial decision of the Plain.

a: what he owes her
t: 'What he owes' or 'the goodwill that is owed'?
p: The KJV's 'due benevolence' comes from a longer Greek text.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: the debt
readings.plain: what he owes her

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: the goodwill that is owed
readings.plain: the goodwill that is owed her

why: The Plain follows the shorter text. "Goodwill" softens a blunt word (the "debt" of marriage) and is probably a scribe's tidying.

a: give yourselves to prayer
p: The KJV says 'fasting and prayer'; the critical editions have only prayer.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: give yourselves to prayer
readings.plain: give yourselves to prayer

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV) add 'fasting and'
readings.orig: σχολάσητε τῇ νηστείᾳ καὶ τῇ προσευχῇ
readings.en: give yourselves to fasting and prayer
readings.plain: give yourselves to fasting and prayer

why: The Plain follows the shorter text. A scribe may have added fasting to prayer, and the shorter text is the harder one to explain as an omission.
b: The last clause also differs: the critical editions have "come together again" with the verb "be" (ēte), while the Byzantine text has "come together" (synerchēsthe). The meaning is the same.

a: in the brother
p: The KJV has 'by the husband'; the critical editions have 'in the brother.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: in the brother
readings.plain: in the brother

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: in the husband
readings.plain: in the husband

why: The Plain follows "brother." The word "husband" is the easier reading, since the rest of the verse speaks of husband and wife, and a copyist could have made it match. "Brother" means a fellow believer, which is the point.

a: God has called us
p: The editions disagree on one letter: 'us' or 'you.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV): 'us'
readings.en: us
readings.plain: God has called us

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort: 'you'
readings.en: you
readings.plain: God has called you

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT. The two Greek words differ by one letter and sound alike, so scribes could mix them up in both directions. "Us" makes the line a general statement; "you" speaks to the Corinthians. The editors split.

a: the Lord has given him, the one he was in when God called him
p: The Byzantine text has 'God has given' and 'the Lord called.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ κύριος ... ὁ θεός
readings.en: as the Lord has assigned ... as God has called
readings.plain: the Lord has given him, the one he was in when God called him

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ θεός ... ὁ κύριος
readings.en: as God has assigned ... as the Lord has called
readings.plain: God has given him, the one he was in when the Lord called him

why: The Plain follows the oldest text. Paul's usual language is that God calls (1:9; 7:15, 24), and the Byzantine reading looks like a copyist making the verse match his usage.
b: Westcott-Hort and Tregelles read a different form of the verb "assigned" (the word list shows they lack the SBLGNT form). It does not change the sense.

a: and he is divided. And the unmarried woman, the virgin,
p: The KJV reads 'There is difference also between a wife and a virgin'; the critical editions read differently.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 ('and he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin ...')
readings.orig: καὶ μεμέρισται. καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος
readings.en: and he is divided. And the woman, the unmarried, and the virgin
readings.plain: and he is divided. And the unmarried woman, the virgin,

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV); the verb begins verse 34 and the wife and the virgin are contrasted
readings.orig: μεμέρισται καὶ ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος. ἡ ἄγαμος
readings.en: There is a difference between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman
readings.plain: There is a difference between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT, and the NA28 text is the same. The Byzantine text divides the sentence differently, which gives the KJV's contrast between a wife and a virgin. Paul goes on to speak of the unmarried woman and the virgin together, which fits the SBLGNT division better. Several smaller variations of word order and punctuation also occur here.
b: The Greek has "and" between "the unmarried woman" and "the virgin" (hē gynē hē agamos kai hē parthenos), with one singular verb. The Plain's comma joins the two as one group; that is a choice, and the literal order is "the unmarried woman and the virgin."

a: the one who sees to the marriage of his virgin
t: 'Gives in marriage' or 'marries' (and where is 'his virgin')?
p: The Byzantine text uses a different verb and leaves out 'his virgin' in 7:38. The Greek verb itself can mean 'give in marriage' or 'marry.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT: gamizōn with 'his virgin'
readings.en: the one giving in marriage (or marrying) his own virgin
readings.plain: the one who sees to the marriage of his virgin

readings.w: Byzantine text: ekgamizōn, with no object
readings.en: the one giving in marriage
readings.plain: the one who gives in marriage

why: The Plain follows the critical text and renders the verb with a wide phrase, "sees to the marriage of." The oldest verb gamizō usually means "give in marriage" (the father reading), but later Greek also uses it for "marry" (the fiancé reading), so one English verb would settle a question the Greek leaves open. The Byzantine ekgamizō is a stronger compound that points to giving in marriage, which is the father reading.
b: The Plain's wording keeps both readings possible. See the note on 7:36 for the four ways of reading the passage.

a: A wife is bound
p: The KJV says 'bound by the law'; the oldest text just says 'bound.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: A wife is bound
readings.plain: A wife is bound

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV) add 'by law'
readings.en: A wife is bound by law
readings.plain: A wife is bound by law

why: The Plain follows the shorter text. The longer reading is the same as Romans 7:2 ("bound by law"), which a scribe would remember. Paul's wording here does not need the word.

a: he has not yet known it the way it must be known
t: 'Has not yet known' or 'knows nothing yet'?
p: The KJV has 'he knows nothing yet'; the critical editions are shorter.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: has not yet known as it is necessary to know
readings.plain: he has not yet known it the way it must be known

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV). The Byzantine text also has a different verb in the first clause (eidenai, 'to know', for egnōkenai)
readings.orig: οὐδέπω οὐδὲν ἔγνωκεν καθὼς δεῖ γνῶναι
readings.en: knows nothing yet as he ought to know
readings.plain: he knows nothing yet the way he ought to know

why: The Plain follows the critical editions. The Byzantine reading is stronger ("nothing"), and a scribe may have sharpened it. The oldest wording is gentler: the knowledge is not yet of the right kind.

a: because they have been used to idols until now
p: The KJV says 'with conscience of the idol'; the critical editions say 'habit.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: τῇ συνηθείᾳ ἕως ἄρτι τοῦ εἰδώλου
readings.en: by the habit until now of the idol
readings.plain: because they have been used to idols until now

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: τῇ συνειδήσει τοῦ εἰδώλου ἕως ἄρτι
readings.en: with the conscience of the idol until now
readings.plain: because they are still conscious of the idol

why: The Plain follows "habit" (synētheia). The two words look almost the same in Greek, and "conscience" (syneidēsis) is the word of the next clause, which could have drawn a scribe's eye. "Habit" gives a clear sense: the weak are used to eating idol food as a sacrifice.
b: The KJV's "with conscience of the idol" can be read as "with consciousness of the idol," which is close in meaning to the habit of seeing it as a god.

a: If we eat, we do not have more. If we do not eat, we do not have less.
p: The editions put the two clauses in different order; the meaning is the same.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV) (eating first)
readings.orig: ἐὰν φάγωμεν, περισσεύομεν ... ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα
readings.en: if we eat we abound ... if we do not eat we lack
readings.plain: If we eat, we do not have more. If we do not eat, we do not have less.

readings.w: NA28, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (not eating first)
readings.orig: ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα ... ἐὰν φάγωμεν, περισσεύομεν
readings.en: if we do not eat we lack ... if we eat we abound
readings.plain: If we do not eat, we do not have less. If we eat, we do not have more.

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT order. The two orders do not change the sense.
b: The KJV follows the eating-first order: "neither, if we eat, are we the better."

a: So the weak person is being destroyed by your knowledge, a brother for whom Christ died.
p: The KJV reads 'And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish'; the critical editions have a present statement.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: ἀπόλλυται γὰρ ὁ ἀσθενῶν ἐν τῇ σῇ γνώσει, ὁ ἀδελφὸς δι' ὃν Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν
readings.en: For the weak person is destroyed in your knowledge, the brother for whom Christ died
readings.plain: So the weak person is being destroyed by your knowledge, a brother for whom Christ died.

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπολεῖται ὁ ἀσθενῶν ἀδελφὸς ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ γνώσει, δι' ὃν Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν
readings.en: And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge, for whom Christ died
readings.plain: And the weak brother will be destroyed by your knowledge, the one for whom Christ died.

why: The Plain follows the critical editions, in the present tense with "for." The Byzantine text has a future, "will perish," as a warning of what might happen; the present tense is more direct: it is happening as the strong eat. A copyist may have softened it.
b: The difference matters for the debate on whether a believer can perish (see the card at 8:11). Both forms speak of "destroying" the weak brother.
